Text:
In eukaryotes, most primary transcripts of protein-coding genes undergo three major modifications {{c2::prior to::prior to or after}} their transport to the cytoplasm for translation:

5′ end → {{c1::a 7-methyl guanosine cap is added}}

3′ end → {{c1::a poly(A) tail is added}}

within the transcript → {{c1::intron sequences are spliced out}}
Back Extra:
Mechanism: the 5′ cap is a 7-methyl guanosine joined to the transcript's initial nucleoside by a 5′-5′ phosphate linkage, and the 3′ poly(A) tail is a polyadenosine tract 20 to 200 nucleotides long.

Pitfall: introns are spliced out only when present; not every gene contains one.
verified_against: p285: 'Moreover, in eukaryotes, the majority of the primary transcripts of genes that encode polypeptides undergo three major modifications prior to their transport to the cytoplasm for translation' | p285: '1. 7-Methyl guanosine caps are added to the 5′ ends of the primary transcripts.' | p285: '2. Poly(A) tails are added to the 3′ ends of the transcripts, which are generated by cleavage rather than by termination of chain extension.' | p285: '3. When present, intron sequences are spliced out of transcripts.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p285: 'The 5′ cap on most eukaryotic mRNAs is a 7-methyl guanosine molecule joined to the initial nucleoside of the transcript by a 5′-5′ phosphate linkage.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p285: 'The 3′ poly(A) tail is a polyadenosine tract 20 to 200 nucleotides long.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275: 'Most of the nuclear genes in higher eukaryotes and some in lower eukaryotes contain noncoding sequences called introns'

must_test: the three modifications: 5′ 7-methyl guanosine cap, 3′ poly(A) tail, intron splicing (grouped c1, each row cued by its position on the transcript)
the modifications happen PRIOR TO transport to the cytoplasm (c2, forced-choice)
the 3′ end is generated by cleavage rather than termination — tested on the sibling cleavage card (unit idx 1)
supporting: cap joined by a 5′-5′ phosphate linkage (unmarked, Back Extra)
poly(A) tail 20 to 200 nucleotides long (unmarked, Back Extra)
'when present' qualifier on introns (Pitfall)
skip: 'the majority of' rendered as 'most' in the stem

Text: The 3′ end of a eukaryotic primary transcript (pre-mRNA) that receives the poly(A) tail is generated by {{c1::cleavage}} of the transcript, rather than by termination of chain extension.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: in E. coli, chain elongation stops when RNA polymerase encounters a transcription-termination signal, so the transcript's end is simply where the enzyme stops.

Pathway: 5′ cap added → transcript cut at the cleavage site and the poly(A) tail added → intron spliced out.
verified_against: p285: '2. Poly(A) tails are added to the 3′ ends of the transcripts, which are generated by cleavage rather than by termination of chain extension.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p285: 'Chain elongation stops when RNA polymerase encounters a transcription–termination signal.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p286 (FIGURE 11.12 text, read on the rendered page): 'Cleavage site' | '2 Poly(A) tail is added.' | '3 Intron is spliced out.'

visual_source.note: the Pathway order and the 'Cleavage site' step were read on the rendered page; the marked numbered list on p285 gives the same order

must_test: the poly(A)-bearing 3′ end is made by CLEAVAGE, not by termination of chain extension (contrast anchor visible per card-rules #21b, so no forced-choice hint is needed)
supporting: E. coli termination-signal contrast (unmarked p285 key point)
processing order cap → cleavage/poly(A) → splicing (figure text)

Text: In eukaryotes, {{c1::heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA)}} is {{c2::the population of primary transcripts in a nucleus}}, so named because of the large variation in the {{c1::sizes}} of the RNA molecules present.
Back Extra:
Why: major portions of hnRNA are noncoding intron sequences that are excised and degraded in the nucleus, so much of it is pre-mRNA caught in mid-processing.

Distinguish: mRNA is the processed product that leaves for the cytoplasm; hnRNA is the raw nuclear population, still carrying its introns.

Cue: eukaryotic transcripts are coated with RNA-binding proteins during or immediately after synthesis, which protects them from ribonucleases during processing and transport.
verified_against: p285: 'In eukaryotes, the population of primary transcripts in a nucleus is called heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA) because of the large variation in the sizes of the RNA molecules present.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p285: 'Major portions of these hnRNAs are noncoding intron sequences, which are excised from the primary transcripts and degraded in the nucleus.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p285: 'Thus, much of the hnRNA actually consists of pre-mRNA molecules undergoing various processing events before leaving the nucleus.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p285: 'Also, in eukaryotes, RNA transcripts are coated with RNA-binding proteins during or immediately after their synthesis.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p285: 'These proteins protect gene transcripts from degradation by ribonucleases, enzymes that degrade RNA molecules, during processing and transport to the cytoplasm.'

must_test: hnRNA ↔ the population of primary transcripts in a nucleus (two-way, c1/c2)
why the name: the large variation in the SIZES of the RNAs (grouped with the term under c1 so the reason cannot decode the term)
supporting: much of hnRNA is intron sequence, excised and degraded in the nucleus (unmarked)
hnRNA is largely pre-mRNA in mid-processing (unmarked)
RNA-binding protein coat protects transcripts from ribonucleases (unmarked)
skip: marks 35 and 36 are two halves of one sentence broken at 'heter|ogeneous' — treated as one span

Text: Unlike the E. coli enzyme, {{c1::all::all, or only some}} eukaryotic RNA polymerases require the assistance of other proteins called {{c2::transcription factors}} in order to initiate the synthesis of RNA chains.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: the transcription factors must bind the promoter and form an initiation complex before the polymerase will bind and begin transcription.

Distinguish: the E. coli enzyme carries its own promoter recognition — its sigma subunit binds the polymerase to the promoter and is released once the chain has started.

Pitfall: different promoters and different transcription factors are used by the different eukaryotic polymerases.
verified_against: p286: 'unlike the E. coli enzyme, all eukaryotic RNA polymerases require the assistance of other proteins called transcription factors in order to initiate the synthesis of RNA chains.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p287: 'Indeed, these transcription factors must bind to a promoter region in DNA and form an appropriate initiation complex before RNA polymerase will bind and initiate transcription.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p287: 'Different promoters and transcription factors are utilized by RNA polymerases.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p281: 'The function of sigma is to recognize and bind RNA polymerase to the transcription initiation or promoter sites in DNA.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p281: 'After RNA chain initiation has occurred, the σ factor is released, and chain elongation (see Figure 11.5) is catalyzed by the core enzyme (α2ββ′).'

must_test: ALL eukaryotic RNA polymerases (not only one) need help to initiate — the qualifier, forced-choice c1
the helper proteins are called transcription factors (c2)
contrast with the E. coli enzyme kept visible as the comparator
supporting: TFs bind the promoter and form an initiation complex before the polymerase binds (unmarked p287)
sigma does promoter recognition for the E. coli enzyme and is released after initiation (unmarked p281)
different promoters/TFs per polymerase (unmarked p287)

Text: Eukaryotes possess {{c1::five::number of enzymes}} different RNA polymerases, each with its own location and its own set of RNA products.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a single RNA polymerase catalyzes all transcription in E. coli.

Pitfall: across eukaryotes the count runs from three to five — RNA polymerases I, II and III are present in most, if not all, eukaryotes, and the fourth and fifth have so far been identified only in plants.
verified_against: p286 (TABLE 11.1 title): 'Characteristics of the Five RNA Polymerases of Eukaryotes' | p286 (TABLE 11.1 columns): 'Enzyme Location Products' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p285: 'Whereas a single RNA polymerase catalyzes all transcription in E. coli, eukaryotes ranging in complexity from the single-celled yeasts to humans contain from three to five different RNA polymerases.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p285: 'Three enzymes, designated RNA polymerases I, II, and III, are known to be present in most, if not all, eukaryotes.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p285: 'Five different RNA polymerases are present in eukaryotes, and each enzyme catalyzes the transcription of a specific class of genes.'

visual_source.note: table read on the rendered page

must_test: the membership count: FIVE eukaryotic RNA polymerases (rule 30 — membership before rows; derived from the marked table's title)
supporting: E. coli uses a single RNA polymerase (unmarked)
three-to-five range across eukaryotes; I, II, III near-universal (unmarked)
skip: 'each enzyme catalyzes the transcription of a specific class of genes' (unmarked; paraphrased only as visible framing from the table's Location/Products columns)

Text: Eukaryotic RNA polymerase {{c1::I::numeral}} synthesizes {{c2::all ribosomal RNAs except the small 5S rRNA}} and is located in the {{c3::nucleolus}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the nucleolus is a distinct region of the nucleus where rRNAs are synthesized and combined with ribosomal proteins, so the rRNA polymerase sits there.

Pitfall: 5S rRNA is still a ribosomal RNA; it is simply the product of a different eukaryotic polymerase.
verified_against: p286 (TABLE 11.1 row): 'RNA polymerase I — Nucleolus — Ribosomal RNAs, excluding 5S rRNA' | p286: 'RNA polymerase I catalyzes the synthesis of all ribosomal RNAs except the small 5S rRNA.' | p286: 'RNA polymerase I is located in the nucleolus, a distinct region of the nucleus where rRNAs are synthesized and combined with ribosomal proteins.' | p286 (TABLE 11.1 row, for the Pitfall): 'RNA polymerase III — Nucleus — tRNAs, 5S rRNA, and other small nuclear RNAs'

visual_source.note: table read on the rendered page

must_test: product → enzyme: which polymerase makes the rRNAs (c1)
enzyme → product: all rRNAs EXCEPT the small 5S rRNA (c2)
location: the nucleolus (c3) — the one location in the table that is not simply 'nucleus'
supporting: what the nucleolus is/does (body prose beside the table)
5S is made by a different polymerase (table row III; the plate on the back names it)
skip: '10 or more subunits' complexity sentence (unmarked, belongs to the earlier p285 marks)

Text: Eukaryotic RNA polymerase {{c1::II::numeral}} is the enzyme that synthesizes the {{c2::nuclear pre-mRNAs::RNA class}}.
Back Extra:
Why: RNA polymerase II transcribes the nuclear genes that encode proteins, and perhaps other genes specifying hnRNAs.

Cue: RNA polymerase II transcribes the vast majority of eukaryotic genes.
verified_against: p286 (TABLE 11.1 row): 'RNA polymerase II — Nucleus — Nuclear pre-mRNAs' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p286: 'RNA polymerase II transcribes nuclear genes that encode proteins and perhaps other genes specifying hnRNAs.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p287: 'In this section, we focus on the initiation of pre-mRNA synthesis by RNA polymerase II, which transcribes the vast majority of eukaryotic genes.'

visual_source.note: table read on the rendered page

must_test: product → enzyme: which polymerase makes the pre-mRNAs (c1)
enzyme → product: nuclear pre-mRNAs (c2)
supporting: Pol II transcribes protein-coding nuclear genes (unmarked)
Pol II transcribes the vast majority of eukaryotic genes (unmarked p287)
skip: location 'Nucleus' — not clozed: 'nuclear' in the product name would make the blank a tautology; the plate carries it

Text: Eukaryotic RNA polymerase {{c1::III::numeral}} synthesizes the {{c2::tRNAs}}, the {{c2::5S rRNA}}, and other {{c2::small nuclear RNAs}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the theme is small RNAs — none of RNA polymerase III's products is a messenger or a large ribosomal RNA.

Pitfall: 5S rRNA is a ribosomal RNA, yet the rRNA-making polymerase of the nucleolus does not produce it.
verified_against: p286 (TABLE 11.1 row): 'RNA polymerase III — Nucleus — tRNAs, 5S rRNA, and other small nuclear RNAs' | p286: 'RNA polymerase III catalyzes the synthesis of the transfer RNA molecules, the 5S rRNA molecules, and small nuclear RNAs.' | p286 (for the Pitfall): 'RNA polymerase I catalyzes the synthesis of all ribosomal RNAs except the small 5S rRNA.'

visual_source.note: table read on the rendered page

must_test: product → enzyme: which polymerase makes tRNA / 5S rRNA / snRNAs (c1)
enzyme → products: the three-member set under one c2 (3 uncued answers, within the ≤4 cap)
supporting: 5S rRNA is the ribosomal RNA NOT made by the nucleolar polymerase (table row I)

Text: Eukaryotic RNA polymerase {{c1::IV::numeral}} synthesizes transcripts that are processed into short RNAs called {{c2::small interfering RNAs (siRNAs)::RNA class}}, important regulators of gene expression that interact with various proteins to {{c3::modify (condense or relax) chromatin structure::mechanism}}.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: RNA polymerases IV and V help turn off the transcription of genes by modifying the structure of chromosomes — chromatin remodeling, in which the histone tails in nucleosomes are chemically modified and proteins bind those modified groups, making the chromatin more or less condensed.

Distinguish: RNA polymerase V also makes a subset of siRNAs, but its signature product is the noncoding (antisense) transcripts of the genes the siRNAs regulate.
verified_against: p286: 'RNA polymerase IV synthesizes transcripts that are processed into short RNAs called small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) that are important regulators of gene expression' | p286: 'These siRNAs interact with various proteins to modify (condense or relax) chromatin structure.' | p286 (TABLE 11.1 row): 'RNA polymerase IV — Nucleus (plant) — Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs)' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p286: 'RNA polymerases IV and V play important roles in turning off the transcription of genes by modifying the structure of chromosomes, a process called chromatin remodeling' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p286: 'Chromatin remodeling occurs when the histone tails in nucleosomes (see Figure 9.18) are chemically modified and proteins interact with these modified groups, causing the chromatin to become more or less condensed.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p286: 'RNA polymerase V synthesizes a subset of siRNAs and noncoding (antisense) transcripts of genes that are regulated by siRNAs.'

visual_source.note: table read on the rendered page

must_test: product → enzyme: Pol IV is the polymerase whose transcripts become siRNAs (c1)
the product class: small interfering RNAs, siRNAs (c2)
what siRNAs do: interact with proteins to modify (condense or relax) chromatin structure (c3)
supporting: siRNAs are important regulators of gene expression (kept visible as the situational cue)
chromatin remodeling = turning genes off by modifying chromosome structure (unmarked)
Pol V makes only a subset of siRNAs plus antisense transcripts (table row V)
skip: location 'Nucleus (plant)' — the plant fact is its own note (unit idx 10)

Text: Eukaryotic RNA polymerase {{c1::V::numeral}} synthesizes some siRNAs plus {{c2::noncoding (antisense) transcripts::kind of RNA}} of the genes that the siRNAs regulate.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: the siRNAs are thought to interact with the antisense transcripts and with nucleosome-associated proteins to condense chromatin into structures that cannot be transcribed.

Distinguish: RNA polymerase IV is the polymerase whose transcripts are processed into siRNAs in the first place; V's own transcripts are what the siRNAs act on.
verified_against: p286 (TABLE 11.1 row): 'RNA polymerase V — Nucleus (plant) — Some siRNAs plus noncoding (antisense) transcripts of siRNA target genes.' | p286: 'RNA polymerase V synthesizes a subset of siRNAs and noncoding (antisense) transcripts of genes that are regulated by siRNAs.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p286: 'it seems likely that the siRNAs interact with these noncoding transcripts and nucleosome-associated proteins—some well characterized, others unknown—to condense chromatin into structures that cannot be transcribed.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p286: 'RNA polymerase IV synthesizes transcripts that are processed into short RNAs called small interfering RNAs (siRNAs)'

visual_source.note: table read on the rendered page

must_test: product → enzyme: the polymerase whose signature product is the antisense transcripts of siRNA target genes (c1)
enzyme → product: noncoding (antisense) transcripts (c2); 'some siRNAs' kept visible because it does not discriminate V from IV
supporting: proposed mechanism: siRNAs + antisense transcripts + nucleosome proteins condense chromatin (unmarked, hedged 'thought to')
skip: 'Although the details of the process are still being worked out' hedge (kept as 'thought to')

Text: Two of the eukaryotic RNA polymerases, {{c1::IV and V::numerals}}, have so far been identified only in {{c2::plants::group of organisms}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: hints exist that RNA polymerases IV and V occur in other eukaryotes too, especially fungi.

Why: both help turn off the transcription of genes by modifying chromosome structure, a process called chromatin remodeling.

Pitfall: RNA polymerases I, II and III are present in most, if not all, eukaryotes; the count across eukaryotes runs from three to five.
verified_against: p286: 'To date, RNA polymerases IV and V have been identified only in plants' | p286 (TABLE 11.1 rows): 'RNA polymerase IV — Nucleus (plant)' | 'RNA polymerase V — Nucleus (plant)' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p286: 'however, there are hints that they may exist in other eukaryotes, especially fungi.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p286: 'RNA polymerases IV and V play important roles in turning off the transcription of genes by modifying the structure of chromosomes, a process called chromatin remodeling' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p285: 'Three enzymes, designated RNA polymerases I, II, and III, are known to be present in most, if not all, eukaryotes.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p285: 'eukaryotes ranging in complexity from the single-celled yeasts to humans contain from three to five different RNA polymerases.'

visual_source.note: table read on the rendered page

must_test: which two polymerases are plant-only: IV and V (c1)
where IV and V have been found: only in plants (c2)
supporting: 'to date' hedge and the fungi hint (unmarked)
IV and V silence genes via chromatin remodeling (unmarked)
I, II, III near-universal (unmarked)
skip: 'plants' deliberately kept OUT of the Pol IV and Pol V row-card stems so this card's c2 is not exposed on its siblings' fronts

Text: {{c1::Reverse transcription::process}} is {{c2::the copying of RNA into complementary DNA}}, which some RNA viruses of eukaryotes are able to carry out.
Back Extra:
Why: the name records that reverse transcription runs the usual DNA → RNA flow of genetic information backwards.

Ex: HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, is the well-known example of a virus that uses reverse transcriptase in its life cycle; some transposable genetic elements in eukaryotic genomes do the same, copying their RNAs into DNA that is then inserted somewhere in the genome.

Cue: sequences derived from reverse transcription make up a large fraction of many eukaryotic genomes — 44 percent of the human genome.
verified_against: p287: 'These viruses possess an enzyme that can copy a molecule of RNA into a complementary molecule of DNA in a process called reverse transcription—because it reverses the flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA.' | p287 (the referent of 'These viruses', unmarked framing only): 'In eukaryotes, some of the RNA viruses have a more elaborate system for expressing their genes and replicating their genomes.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p287: 'The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), is a well-known example of a virus that uses reverse transcriptase in its life cycle.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p287: 'Some of the transposable genetic elements found in eukaryotic genomes also make use of reverse transcriptases. The RNAs transcribed from these elements are copied into DNA molecules, which are then inserted somewhere in the genome.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p287: 'Genome sequencing projects have revealed that a large fraction of many eukaryotic genomes consists of sequences derived from reverse transcription—in humans, for example, 44 percent.'

must_test: reverse transcription ↔ copying RNA into complementary DNA (two-way, c1/c2)
why the name: it reverses the DNA → RNA flow (Back Extra Why — by meaning it is the same fact as the c2 definition, so it is not clozed twice)
supporting: HIV and transposable elements use reverse transcriptase (unmarked)
44 percent of the human genome derives from reverse transcription (unmarked, numeric)

Text: An enzyme that copies RNA into DNA is formally an {{c1::RNA-dependent DNA polymerase::formal name}}, though it is usually just called a {{c2::reverse transcriptase::common name}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: read the name as template-dependent product-polymerase — an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase uses an RNA template to make DNA, the mirror image of ordinary transcription's DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

Distinguish: an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase copies RNA into RNA and makes no DNA; RNA viruses such as influenza use one to make their mRNAs and replicate their genomes, and eukaryotic cells use their own to make small regulatory RNAs.
verified_against: p287: 'Enzymes that copy RNA into DNA are RNA-dependent DNA polymerases, but often they are simply called reverse transcriptases.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p287: 'RNA viruses that infect eukaryotic cells use an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to produce mRNAs that encode viral proteins and to replicate their genomes. The virus that causes influenza in humans is an example.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p286: 'Eukaryotes also possess enzymes that use a molecule of RNA as a template to synthesize a complementary molecule of RNA. These RNA-dependent RNA polymerases are involved in the production of small RNA molecules that regulate gene expression.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275 (FIGURE 11.1 text): 'DNA-dependent RNA polymerase' | 'RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase)'

must_test: the enzyme's formal name: RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (c1)
its common name: reverse transcriptase (c2)
supporting: naming convention template → product (reading aid)
RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (influenza; eukaryotic small-RNA production) as the confusable (unmarked)
